title: Understanding the Command Line. Long Live the Command Line!
summary: Explains what a shell is, what Bash is, and why developers prefer the command line to graphical file managers.

concepts.heading: Kernel and shell
points: The kernel is the core of the operating system and is the program that talks directly to hardware.
A shell is the interface a person uses to reach the kernel. It comes in two kinds: graphical (e.g. Finder or Explorer) and command line interface (CLI).
Bash (Bourne Again Shell) is a command line interpreter for Unix-style systems.

concepts.heading: Where Unix lives
points: Linux is Unix-like, most servers run Unix-like systems, and macOS is Unix-based too.
Windows comes from a different lineage (DOS), which is why Windows users install Git Bash to get the same commands.

concepts.heading: Why use the command line
points: Control: you steer the machine more directly than through a GUI.
Speed: creating a folder is one short command (mkdir Music), and the up arrow recalls the previous command so a variation (Music2) takes seconds.
Visibility: GUIs hide config files and dot-folders; ls -a shows hidden entries, and a folder starting with a dot (mkdir .Secrets) is hidden by default.
Git and version control, taught later, are used mostly from the command line.

code_examples.caption: Create a folder, then list including hidden items

pitfalls: Do not confuse the kernel (hardware-facing core) with the shell (user-facing layer).

gaps_and_ideas: Proposed new lesson 'What is the command line?' Blurb: the shell is the layer you use to talk to the kernel; a GUI file manager and a CLI like Bash are two shells over the same files, and the CLI adds speed, control and access to hidden files.

Tasks: (1) in the simulated terminal, run mkdir Music and see the folder appear in a mirrored 'Finder' panel; (2) press the Up arrow to recall the command and edit it to mkdir Music2; (3) run mkdir .Secrets and notice it does not show in ls or the GUI panel; (4) run ls -a to reveal it, plus the . and .. entries; (5) match three terms (kernel, shell, Bash) to their definitions.

Starter code idea: a JS object representing a fake home folder (Desktop, Documents, Downloads, .config) and a tiny command parser supporting mkdir, ls and ls -a, with a history array driving Up/Down arrow recall.

Interactive demo: a split view with a layered diagram (hardware > kernel > shell > user) on one side and the terminal plus a GUI-style folder view on the other, where every command typed updates both views and highlights which layer handled it.
